questions.title: What exactly is the "hyperspherical energy" used in OFT, and why does the paper define it as a sum of inverse distances rather than cosine similarities?
questions.question_body: In Section 1 and 3, the paper motivates preserving pairwise "hyperspherical similarity" (e.g., cosine similarity), but then defines hyperspherical energy for a layer W as HE(W) = \sum_{i \ne j} \|\hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j\|^{-1}, where \hat{w}_i = w_i / \|w_i\|. This looks like a sum over inverse Euclidean distances on the unit sphere, not cosine similarities. Why this particular choice (inverse distance) instead of, say, a function of cosine angles like \sum_{i \ne j} f(\langle \hat{w}_i, \hat{w}_j \rangle)? Is there a theoretical or empirical reason this specific energy better captures the "semantic" structure they want to preserve? Also, since the inverse distance diverges when two normalized neurons coincide, how is that handled in practice?

questions.title: How does an orthogonal left-multiplication preserve the hyperspherical energy defined as a sum of inverse pairwise distances?
questions.question_body: The method applies a layer-wise orthogonal matrix R to a pretrained weight matrix W^0, i.e., W = R W^0, and claims this preserves pairwise angles and thus the hyperspherical energy HE(W). For the energy HE(W) = \sum_{i \ne j} \|\hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j\|^{-1} with \hat{w}_i = w_i/\|w_i\|, can someone provide a short proof that HE(R W^0) = HE(W^0)? My attempt: orthogonal R preserves norms, so \|R w_i\| = \|w_i\| and hence \hat{w}_i' = R \hat{w}_i. Orthogonal maps preserve Euclidean distances, so \|\hat{w}_i' - \hat{w}_j'\| = \|R(\hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j)\| = \|\hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j\|. Therefore each term is unchanged. Is this the full argument, even when R is block-diagonal and shared?

questions.title: Does Cayley parameterization limit OFT by excluding reflections (determinant -1), and does that matter?
questions.question_body: The paper notes the Cayley transform R = (I + Q)(I - Q)^{-1} with skew-symmetric Q generates only special orthogonal matrices with \det(R) = 1 (no reflections). Yet the invariance claim earlier would allow any orthogonal transform, including reflections (\det = -1). Is there any scenario where restricting to \det(R) = 1 reduces expressivity or harms finetuning? If reflections are sometimes beneficial, is there a simple modification (e.g., pre-/post-multiplying by a fixed Householder reflection) to restore access to all of O(d) while keeping the parameterization efficient and differentiable?

questions.title: How should I interpret the block-diagonal R in OFT for fully-connected vs. convolution layers?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.3, R \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} is parameterized as block-diagonal with r blocks, reducing parameters from \mathcal{O}(d^2) to \mathcal{O}(d^2 / r). For a linear layer W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n} with columns as neurons, left-multiplication R W^0 acts in the input dimension d. For a convolution layer with kernel size k \times k, in-channels c_{in}, and out-channels c_{out}, what exactly are d and n? Is it d = c_{in} k^2 and n = c_{out}? If so, when the paper says a block per input channel resembles depthwise behavior, is each block of size k^2? Could you clarify the exact tensor reshaping and block sharing scheme for convolutions so that the geometric interpretation is precise?

questions.title: Is OFT’s parameter complexity really better than LoRA’s in typical attention layers?
questions.question_body: The paper compares LoRA’s parameter count r'(d+n) with OFT’s \mathcal{O}(d^2/r) for a layer W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}. In attention, W is often square (d = n), or sometimes tall. In realistic Transformer blocks where Q/K/V/O projections are size d_{model} \times d_{model}, what ranges of r (blocks) and r' (rank) make OFT have fewer parameters than LoRA? Also, since OFT’s parameter count is independent of n, when does that help or hurt relative to LoRA on rectangular layers (e.g., when n \gg d)? A worked example for typical Stable Diffusion v1.5 attention dimensions would be helpful.

questions.title: How is the COFT constraint \|R - I\| \le \epsilon enforced in practice, and which norm is used?
questions.question_body: COFT adds the constraint \|R - I\| \le \epsilon in addition to orthogonality, and then maps it to \|Q\| \le \epsilon' via the Cayley approximation R \approx I + 2Q + \mathcal{O}(Q^2). Which norm is used here (spectral or Frobenius)? Under what conditions does the Neumann series-based approximation justify that a bound on \|Q\| enforces a bound on \|R - I\|, and what are the bounds on the approximation error? Is there a principled way to choose \epsilon and \epsilon' to guarantee the constraint holds throughout training?

questions.title: Is the Neumann series approximation for the Cayley transform well-justified when Q is skew-symmetric?
questions.question_body: COFT notes R = (I + Q)(I - Q)^{-1} and uses a Neumann series to approximate (I - Q)^{-1} by \sum_{k \ge 0} Q^k, yielding R \approx I + 2Q + \mathcal{O}(Q^2). For real skew-symmetric Q, the eigenvalues are purely imaginary. While I - Q is always invertible, the Neumann series converges only if \|Q\| < 1 in the chosen operator norm. Since COFT also constrains \|Q\| \le \epsilon', is the approximation error controllably small for practical \epsilon'? Do the authors actually compute the exact inverse (I - Q)^{-1} during training, or do they rely on truncated series or iterative inversion (e.g., Newton–Schulz)?

questions.title: In the re-scaled OFT variant, why does right-multiplying by a diagonal D not change hyperspherical energy?
questions.question_body: The re-scaled OFT uses z = (R W^0 D)^\top x with a diagonal D = \text{diag}(s_1, \dots, s_n), s_i > 0. If hyperspherical energy HE(W) is defined as a function of normalized columns \hat{w}_i = w_i / \|w_i\|, then scaling column i by s_i does not change \hat{w}_i. Is the claim simply that column-wise positive scalings cancel out in the normalization, so HE(R W^0 D) = HE(R W^0)? Are there any caveats if some s_i become very small or large during optimization (e.g., numerical issues, effective learning rate coupling)?

questions.title: How exactly is OFT applied within Stable Diffusion v1.5’s U-Net and attention blocks?
questions.question_body: For a fair comparison to LoRA, the paper says OFT is applied to the same attention weights LoRA uses. Concretely: which specific linear projections receive the orthogonal left-multiplication R (Q, K, V, O, or some subset)? Are biases present and, if so, are they frozen or also transformed? Is R shared across heads, per-head, per-layer, or shared across layers? If multiple R’s exist, are they all constrained via Cayley and optionally block-diagonal, or only a subset?

questions.title: If OFT is equivalent to adding (R - I)W^0 to W^0, when is (R - I) low-rank in practice?
questions.question_body: The paper remarks that OFT’s update can be written as W = W^0 + (R - I)W^0 and "also performs low-rank weight update when R - I is low-rank." However, a generic orthogonal R will have full rank and (R - I) often also has rank close to d. Under the block-diagonal parameterization, is there any reason to expect (R - I) to be low-rank, or is the analogy to LoRA mainly conceptual? Is there an empirical measurement of \text{rank}((R - I)W^0) or its singular value decay after finetuning?

questions.title: What is meant by "layer-shared orthogonal transformation": shared within a layer, or shared across layers?
questions.question_body: Several places say OFT learns a "layer-shared orthogonal transformation for neurons". I read this as: within a given layer W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}, a single R \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} multiplies all columns of that W. However, it could also be misread as sharing the same R across multiple layers. Which interpretation is correct? If R is shared across layers with different input dimensions d, how is that handled? If not shared across layers, is there any benefit to sharing R across a group of layers with the same d?

questions.title: How is the control consistency metric computed for C2I, S2I, and L2F, and how sensitive is it to the choice of estimator?
questions.question_body: For controllable generation, the paper proposes to "estimate the control signal from the generated image and then compare it with the original control signal." For Canny-to-image, what edge detector and thresholding is used on the generated image, and how are IoU/F1 computed against the original edges? For segmentation-to-image, what semantic segmentation model is used to re-estimate the segmentation (architecture, training dataset, accuracy), and does its bias favor some styles over others? For landmark-to-face, what landmark detector is used and how robust is the \ell_2 error to slight appearance changes? Could different choices of estimators significantly change the relative ranking of methods?

questions.title: Why does "OFT without the orthogonality constraint" fail so catastrophically in the ablation?
questions.question_body: Figure 3 (orthogonality ablation) shows that relaxing the orthogonality constraint leads to training collapse. What exactly is the non-orthogonal parameterization used there? Is it still a left-multiplication by an unconstrained matrix A, i.e., W = A W^0, or is A added to W^0? If it is W = A W^0, could the collapse be due to uncontrolled scaling and shearing that dramatically change layer Lipschitz constants? Did the authors try normalizing A (e.g., spectral normalization) or adding a penalty to preserve pairwise angles approximately, to test whether orthogonality itself or angle preservation is the key factor?

questions.title: What norm is used in the COFT projection step on Q, and how is the projection implemented?
questions.question_body: COFT enforces \|Q\| \le \epsilon' by projected gradient descent. Which norm is used (Frobenius, spectral)? If spectral norm is used, is the projection implemented via power iteration to estimate \|Q\|_2 and scaling Q if needed? If Frobenius, is the projection a simple rescaling when \|Q\|_F > \epsilon'? Also, since Q must be skew-symmetric, is the skew-symmetry enforced each step by setting Q \leftarrow (Q - Q^\top)/2 before projection?

questions.title: Does preserving hyperspherical energy guarantee preservation of downstream generative semantics, or is it just a heuristic regularizer?
questions.question_body: The paper argues empirically that preserving hyperspherical energy correlates with preserving "semantic generation ability" of text-to-image diffusion models. Is there any theoretical support that invariance of pairwise angles among normalized neurons suffices to preserve the mapping learned by a diffusion model, at least locally? Could two networks with identical HE but different neuron alignments produce very different outputs? I am trying to understand whether HE preservation is a necessary, sufficient, or just a helpful but non-unique surrogate constraint.

questions.title: How stable is OFT when neurons are near-parallel, given the 1/\|\hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j\| energy term can explode?
questions.question_body: Because HE(W) sums terms of the form \|\hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j\|^{-1}, if \hat{w}_i \approx \hat{w}_j, this term becomes large. Is this ever an issue in pretrained diffusion models (e.g., highly redundant channels)? Do you add a small \delta to the denominator during any diagnostic calculation, or is HE only used conceptually and never explicitly computed during training? If HE is not explicitly computed, how do we ensure training cannot accidentally move the network into a regime with new near-collisions of neuron directions if R is block-diagonal and shared?

questions.title: How does OFT interact with LayerNorm, residual connections, and scale conventions in the U-Net?
questions.question_body: In diffusion U-Nets, linear layers appear inside attention blocks with LayerNorm and residual connections. If we replace W^0 by R W^0, does this effectively change the layer’s operator norm or scaling in a way that affects LayerNorm statistics or residual balance? The ablation with non-orthogonal transforms collapses—could this be tied to violating scale invariances assumed by LayerNorm? Did the authors observe any need to retune normalization parameters or learning rates when switching from standard finetuning/LoRA to OFT?

questions.title: What is the exact training objective for subject-driven OFT and COFT, and how are priors/prompt losses combined?
questions.question_body: For the DreamBooth-like setup, you mention using the same loss as DreamBooth: a reconstruction loss with class-specific prior preservation. Could you spell out the exact objective used with OFT/COFT, including any KL guidance or classifier-free guidance terms? Are text encoder weights frozen? Are there any OFT-specific regularizers (e.g., weight decay on Q or D in re-scaled OFT)? I want to ensure I can reproduce the reported stability and convergence with the same loss and optimizer hyperparameters.

questions.title: Does the claimed compositionality of orthogonal finetunes hold in practice when composing multiple R matrices?
questions.question_body: In the concluding remarks, the paper suggests a compositionality idea: if two OFT finetunes learn orthogonal matrices R_1 and R_2 for the same layer, then R_2 R_1 is still orthogonal and might combine the two task adaptations. But multiplication is non-commutative and COFT’s \|R - I\| constraint might be exceeded after composition. Have the authors tested whether composing multiple R’s preserves performance across tasks, or whether catastrophic interference still occurs? Is there a criterion (e.g., approximate commutativity, small angles) under which composition is likely to work?

questions.title: What exactly is being frozen vs. finetuned in controllable generation experiments, and how is the control signal integrated?
questions.question_body: For ControlNet and T2I-Adapter the control signal is integrated via additional modules. For OFT and COFT, since there is no extra inference-time module, how do you feed the control signal during training? Is it concatenated to the input latents, injected through cross-attention with a conditioning encoder, or encoded into the text prompt? Which parts of the model are frozen vs. receive orthogonal finetunes? A concise description of the data flow and which layers get an R would clarify how OFT achieves control without extra modules.
